benchmark_name: MIThinker: A Plug-and-Play Policy-Optimized Thinker For Motivational Interviewing Counseling
authors: Yizhe Yang; Palakorn Achananuparp; Heyan Huang; Jing Jiang; Ee-Peng Lim
institutions: Beijing Institute of Technology; Singapore Management University; Australian National University
ground_truth_source: AnnoMI dataset (Wu et al., 2022, 2023) — 110 high-quality expert-annotated MI counseling sessions with annotated MI strategy labels; oracle thoughts reverse-engineered via GPT-4o pipeline (AugR1-MI)
size_of_benchmark: 2,322 context-response pairs from 110 sessions; 31,444 oracle thoughts derived; test set: 258 context-response pairs from 10 sessions
what_assessed_skills: MI counseling competency; Theory of Mind (ToM) assessment (belief, desire, intention, emotion, trust); MI strategy selection and alignment; therapeutic reasoning; response generation quality; change talk elicitation
tasks_assessed: Counselor thought generation (ToM assessment + MI strategy reasoning); MI counseling response generation; MI strategy classification; simulated client interaction; session-level MI competency evaluation
population_represented: Simulated counseling clients with diverse behavior change topics (health, economy, relationship, law, education); based on staged AnnoMI demonstrations by trained actors
evaluation_method: Both (Automated + Human). Automated: behavior code classifier (R/Q, %OQ, %CR, %MIC, %TTT); GPT-4o MITI global scores (Cultivating Change Talk, Softening Sustain Talk, Partnership, Empathy on 5-point Likert); BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, Strategy Fit Ratio, Bias; success rate. Human: 10 MI experts assessed thought quality (ToM accuracy, strategy rationality), pairwise thought comparisons, and session-level MITI ratings across 60 contexts and 30 sessions per method.
llms_evaluated: GPT-4o; LLaMA3-70B (LLaMA 3.1 70B); LLaMA3-3B-Instruct (MIThinker backbone); DeepSeek-R1 distilled model (R1-Dist); MindfulMI_SFT (LLaMA3-3B fine-tuned with SFT); MindfulMI_SFT+RL (LLaMA3-3B fine-tuned with SFT+GRPO); CAMI (Yang et al., 2025, multi-module)
mental_health_conditions: Substance use / behavior change (alcohol consumption reduction, smoking cessation, drug use, marijuana use); motivational interviewing for general behavior change motivation
performance_scores: MindfulMI (GPT-4o backbone): R/Q=1.17, %OQ=72.1%, %CR=63.1%, %MIC=94.7%, %TTT=44.1%; MITI global scores ~3.07–3.17; success rate=46.8%; BLEU-2=7.26, ROUGE-L=19.04, BERTScore=88.90, SFR=44.04. MIThinker thought accuracy: Belief=0.80, Intention=0.81 (vs oracle 0.71, 0.78). Expert session evaluation: MindfulMI comparable to CAMI across CCT, SST, PAT, EMP, REA dimensions.
short_summary: This paper proposes MIThinker, a lightweight plug-and-play thinking model that generates explicit therapeutic counselor thoughts (Theory of Mind assessment + MI strategy reasoning) to guide LLM-based Motivational Interviewing (MI) counseling agents. To address the absence of counselor thought data, the authors build the AugR1-MI dataset (31,444 oracle thoughts from 110 AnnoMI sessions) via an automated reverse-engineering pipeline using GPT-4o. MIThinker is trained on LLaMA3-3B-Instruct via two-stage SFT and GRPO reinforcement learning with composite reward functions (format, alignment, reasonableness). The resulting MindfulMI agent is evaluated on simulated MI sessions using automated metrics (MITI behavior codes, BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore, success rate) and human expert annotation (ToM accuracy, pairwise thought comparison, session MITI ratings). MindfulMI achieves MI competency comparable to state-of-the-art CAMI with an order of magnitude less computation, and MIThinker outperforms oracle thoughts on several ToM dimensions.

benchmark_name: Functional outcomes and naturalistic engagement with a purpose-built conversational AI for mental health (Ash)
authors: Kristen M. Van Swearingen; Thomas D. Hull; Karthik V. Sarma; Caitlin A. Stamatis
institutions: Health Psychology Doctoral Program, The University of North Carolina at Charlotte; Slingshot AI, New York, NY; AI in Mental Health Research Group, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, University of California, San Francisco
ground_truth_source: In-app single-item validated questionnaire responses from real-world users (self-report), collected at baseline and Week 4; drawn from validated measures (OECD well-being item, Snyder et al. sleep quality scale, Atroszko et al. relationship satisfaction item, Joseph et al. behavioral activation item, Specific Psychotic Experiences Questionnaire grandiosity subscale, Working Alliance Inventory goals subscale)
size_of_benchmark: 1,284 participants; 6 outcome measures × 2 time points; 4 engagement metrics
what_assessed_skills: Psychological functioning outcomes of a purpose-built conversational AI for mental health (Ash): life satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, sleep quality, behavioral activation, working alliance, grandiosity (inflated self-perception); engagement-outcome associations
tasks_assessed: Within-person change in psychological functioning (life satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, sleep quality, behavioral activation) over 4 weeks of AI chatbot use; within-person change in working alliance and grandiosity; association of engagement metrics (active days, total sessions, total user messages, total session minutes) with Week 4 outcomes
population_represented: Real-world adult users of the Ash mental health AI app who onboarded January–June 2026; distressed/subclinical population (below-average life satisfaction, fair sleep quality); demographics available for subset (n=91): majority female (73.6%), age range 18–65+, primarily 35–54
evaluation_method: Automated (statistical): paired-sample t-tests for within-person change (baseline to Week 4); ANCOVAs for engagement-outcome associations controlling for baseline. Metrics: Cohen's d, % change, t-statistics, p-values, partial R². User self-report questionnaires collected in-app. — Automated
llms_evaluated: Ash (purpose-built conversational AI for mental health by Slingshot AI; base model and architecture not specified in paper)
mental_health_conditions: General psychological distress (subclinical/non-clinical); stress; sleep difficulties; interpersonal challenges; worry; no specific clinical diagnoses assessed
performance_scores: Life satisfaction: d=0.20, +10.16% (p<.001); Relationship satisfaction: d=0.25, +11.63% (p<.001); Sleep quality: d=0.26, +14.69% (p<.001); Behavioral activation: d=0.14, +5.58% (p<.001); Working alliance: d=0.20, +7.73% (p<.001); Grandiosity: d=-0.02, -0.75% (p=0.477, ns). Engagement partial R² range: 0.58–2.15% across significant predictors.
short_summary: This observational cohort study examined within-person changes in psychological functioning among 1,284 real-world users of Ash, a purpose-built conversational AI for mental health, over four weeks of naturalistic use. The study assessed life satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, sleep quality, behavioral activation, working alliance, and grandiosity at baseline and Week 4 using validated single-item in-app measures. Significant improvements were found across all psychological functioning indicators and working alliance (d=0.14–0.26, all p<.001), with no change in grandiosity. Evaluation was fully automated using paired-sample t-tests and ANCOVAs with engagement metrics as predictors. Consistency of engagement (active days, total sessions, total session minutes) predicted better Week 4 outcomes, while message volume did not, suggesting regularity of use matters more than conversation depth for functioning improvements.

benchmark_name: From Black-Box to Clinical Insight: A Multi-Stage Explainable Framework for Speech-Based Cognitive Impairment Detection
authors: Yasaman Haghbin; Sina Rashidi; Ali Zolnour; Fatemeh Taherinezhad; Ali Fartoot; Hossein Azadmaleki; James M Noble; Maryam Dadkhah; Maryam Zolnoori
institutions: Independent Researcher; Columbia University, United States; Chalmers University of Technology, Sweden
ground_truth_source: NIA PREPARE benchmark dataset — speech recordings from 2,058 participants (1,646 training, 412 testing) labeled as Control, MCI, or AD; sourced from multiple corpora
size_of_benchmark: 2,058 participants (1,646 training, 412 testing); 70 English samples used for clinical validity evaluation of explainability framework
what_assessed_skills: Explainability of cognitive impairment detection: SHAP-based token attribution mapped to cognitive-linguistic dimensions (lexical richness, syntactic complexity, disfluencies/repetition, semantic coherence, spatial reasoning difficulty, executive function); clinical interpretability of LLM-generated narratives; usability for clinical workflow integration
tasks_assessed: Speech-based cognitive impairment detection (Control vs. MCI vs. AD classification); SHAP token attribution; LLM-based clinical narrative generation (4-stage pipeline); physician evaluation of explanation alignment with patient cognitive profiles
population_represented: Adults with cognitive impairment (MCI, AD) and healthy controls; 1,140 controls, 268 MCI, 650 AD; English, Spanish, Mandarin speakers; age groups: mid-life (46–65), older adults (66–80), elderly (80+)
languages: English, Spanish, Mandarin (dataset); explainability evaluation on English only (70 samples)
evaluation_method: Both — Automated: SpeechCARE-AGF model evaluated on NIA PREPARE test set (AUC, F1-score); Human: Two primary care physicians independently evaluated LLM-generated explanation reports for 70 stratified English samples under blinded conditions (inter-rater agreement via Cohen's κ); usability assessed by 5 clinicians via System Usability Scale (SUS) and think-aloud sessions
performance_scores: Screening model (SpeechCARE-AGF): AUC = 86.83%, F1 = 72.11% on NIA PREPARE test set; Physician agreement on explainability reports: 98% agreement, Cohen's κ = 0.85; System Usability Scale (SUS): 82/100
short_summary: This paper proposes a multi-stage explainability framework that converts black-box transformer predictions for speech-based cognitive impairment detection into clinically interpretable narratives. The framework integrates SHAP-based token attribution, theory-informed linguistic feature extraction across four cognitive-linguistic dimensions, and a four-stage sequential LLM reasoning pipeline using LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct. It is built on top of the SpeechCARE-AGF multimodal screening model (F1=72.11%, AUC=86.83%) evaluated on the NIA PREPARE benchmark dataset (2,058 participants with Control, MCI, and AD labels). Clinical validity was assessed by two blinded physicians on 70 stratified English samples, yielding 98% agreement (Cohen's κ=0.85), and a usability study with 5 clinicians produced a SUS score of 82/100, indicating strong potential for clinical workflow integration.
